title: Block close: your voice
hook: every generation adds its voice to the conversation
tomorrow: can a rule of just three lines hold a whole life?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Talmud page: every generation around the center, the losing views kept. One long conversation. Today the later voices close, and the open seat at the edge turns toward you.

A song you wrote gets covered by someone you've never met, and they change the chords. You'd expect to be annoyed. The Talmud tells a stranger version. Moses goes up to receive the Torah and finds God tying little crowns onto the letters. Why? Because one day, a man named Akiva will draw heaps of teaching from every one of those crowns. Moses asks to see him, and finds himself sitting at the back of Rabbi Akiva's class. And he can't follow it. The man who brought the Torah down can't follow the lesson. So why does the story say he was comforted?
screen: `SOMEONE COVERS YOUR SONG.` → `CROWNS ON THE LETTERS.` → `MOSES CAN'T FOLLOW THE CLASS.` → `WHY IS HE COMFORTED?`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of it, from tractate Menachot. Moses sits there, lost, and his strength leaves him. Then a student asks Rabbi Akiva, how do you know this? And Akiva answers: it is a teaching given to Moses at Sinai. And Moses is comforted. Solve the puzzle and you have this whole block. Moses doesn't recognize the words, but he recognizes the root. The new teaching grows out of what he was given. It's his, said in a voice he never had. That's how the tradition sees itself: not a sealed box, but a root that keeps putting out new branches, each one honest about where it came from. Look at the voices these weeks: Hasidic joy, Soloveitchik's details, Nechama Leibowitz's real question, Sephardi custom restored, Heschel's wonder, Buber's you, Fackenheim's crooked candle, Wiesel's questions, women's words in three languages. None of them repeated Moses. All of them stood on him. Pirkei Avot adds the last piece. Rabbi Tarfon says, it isn't on you to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either. Nobody has to say the final word. Each generation only has to say its own. So that's the close of this block. The later voices are done, and the next voice in the conversation is yours. Add your voice.
screen: `A TEACHING GIVEN TO MOSES.` · `HE KNOWS THE ROOT.` · `NEW BRANCHES, HONEST ROOTS.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH.` · then, large: `ADD YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write one teaching of your own, a single sentence you've learned from your life and believe is worth passing on. Underneath it, write where it comes from: a person, a text, a hard week. Read both lines back once, slowly.
screen: `ONE TEACHING, ONE SENTENCE.` · `WHERE IT COMES FROM.` · `READ IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Block close: the end of the later voices. Moses at the back of Akiva's class, comforted, because the new teaching grew from his root.
Your line: add your voice, honest about its root. The later voices are done; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: A new insight in Torah study is called a chiddush, and learners share them at Shabbat tables and in study halls, often naming the teacher or text they built on.

fork.setup: your little sister rewrites the family's Passover song with new verses about her school. grandma frowns. what does Moses in Akiva's class suggest?
options: let her add it, as long as the old song is still the root underneath.
stop her; changing a song means losing the tradition.
throw out the old song and use only hers from now on.
fork.reveal: Moses didn't recognize Akiva's words, but he recognized the root, and was comforted. new voices that honor the root are how the conversation continues.

chat.says: program wants a one-line "artist statement." everything i write sounds like someone else said it first.
options: That's ok. Say it in your words and name your roots; that's how a voice gets added.
Then skip it. If it's been said before, there's nothing left for you to add.
Find a line nobody's ever said. Only a totally new idea counts as your voice.
chat.meaning: Akiva's teaching grew from Moses's root, and Moses was comforted. A new voice doesn't have to come from nowhere.

Akiva.meaning: Rabbi Akiva, a great sage of the Mishnah

Menachot.meaning: a Talmud tractate; it tells of Moses in Akiva's class

Sinai.meaning: the mountain where the Torah was given

Pirkei Avot.meaning: Chapters of the Fathers: sayings of the sages

Tarfon.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah quoted in Pirkei Avot
